title: Electricity
subject: Science

items: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charges through a conductor.
Electric current is represented by \(I\).
If a charge \(Q\) flows through a conductor in time \(t\), then:
SI unit of electric current: ampere (A).
1 ampere is the current when 1 coulomb of charge flows through a conductor in 1 second.

blocks.text: Electric current flows through a conductor only when there is a closed conducting path.
An electric circuit is a continuous and closed path through which electric current flows. A simple electric circuit consists of:

items: Electric cell/battery – provides electrical energy.
Connecting wires – provide a path for current.
Switch – opens or closes the circuit.
Electric appliance/load – uses electrical energy.
Conventional direction of current: From the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell through the external circuit.
The actual flow of electrons is opposite to the conventional direction of current.
Electric potential: The electric potential at a point is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point.
Electric potential is represented by \(V\):
Where \(V\) = electric potential, \(W\) = work done, and \(Q\) = charge.
SI unit of electric potential: volt (V).

blocks.text: Potential difference between two points is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to another:

items: The SI unit of potential difference is volt (V).
1 volt is the potential difference when 1 joule of work is done to move 1 coulomb of charge:
Potential difference is measured using a voltmeter.
A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component whose potential difference is to be measured.
A cell or battery provides the potential difference needed to make electric current flow in a circuit.

blocks.text: A circuit diagram is a graphical representation of an electric circuit using standard electrical symbols.

items: Electric cell: Represents a source of electrical energy.
Battery: Combination of two or more cells.
Switch: Used to open or close the circuit.
Bulb: Converts electrical energy into light and heat.
Resistor: Offers resistance to the flow of electric current.
Ammeter: Measures electric current and is connected in series.
Voltmeter: Measures potential difference and is connected in parallel.
A closed circuit allows electric current to flow.
An open circuit does not allow electric current to flow.
Circuit diagrams make electrical circuits easy to understand and analyse.

blocks.text: Ohm’s law: At constant temperature, the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends.

items: \(V\) = potential difference (volt)
\(I\) = electric current (ampere)
\(R\) = resistance (ohm)
The SI unit of resistance is ohm (\(\Omega\)).
A conductor has a resistance of \(1\ \Omega\) if a potential difference of \(1\text{ V}\) produces a current of \(1\text{ A}\) through it:
The \(V\text{–}I\) graph for an ohmic conductor is a straight line passing through the origin.
Ohm's law is valid when the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant.

notes.heading: 11.5 Factors on which the Resistance of the Conductor Depends

blocks.text: The resistance of a conductor depends on the following factors:
Resistance is directly proportional to the length of the conductor:

items: Longer conductor → greater resistance.
Shorter conductor → smaller resistance.

blocks.text: Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section:

items: Thicker conductor → smaller resistance.
Thinner conductor → greater resistance.

blocks.text: Different materials have different resistances. This property is represented by resistivity (\(\rho\)).
The resistance of most metallic conductors increases when temperature increases.

items: \(R\) = resistance
\(\rho\) = resistivity of the material
\(l\) = length of conductor
\(A\) = area of cross-section
Resistivity is a property of a material that indicates how strongly it opposes the flow of electric current.
SI unit of resistivity is ohm-metre (\(\Omega\text{ m}\)).
Resistivity depends on the nature of the material and temperature, but not on the length or thickness of the conductor.

notes.heading: 11.6 Resistance of a System of Resistors

blocks.text: In an electric circuit, two or more resistors can be connected in different ways. The two common methods are:

items: Series combination
Parallel combination
The overall resistance of the combination is called equivalent resistance or effective resistance.
Equivalent resistance is the resistance that can replace the entire combination without changing the current and voltage relationship in the circuit.
Resistors are said to be connected in series when they are connected one after another in a single path.
The same current flows through every resistor.
The total potential difference is the sum of the potential differences across each resistor:

blocks.text: Therefore, resistance in series is greater than the resistance of any individual resistor.

items: Resistors are said to be connected in parallel when their ends are connected to the same two points of a circuit.
The same potential difference acts across each resistor.
The total current is the sum of the currents through the individual resistors:

blocks.text: The equivalent resistance in parallel is less than the smallest individual resistance.

items: When an electric current flows through a resistance, electrical energy is converted into heat energy.
This is called the heating effect of electric current.

blocks.text: The heat produced in a resistor is given by:

items: \(H\) = heat produced
\(I\) = current
\(R\) = resistance
\(t\) = time

blocks.text: Using Ohm's law, \(V = IR\), the heat produced can also be written as:
From \(H = I^2 R t\), heat produced depends on:

items: Square of current (\(I^2\)) — greater current → greater heat produced.
Resistance (\(R\)) — greater resistance → greater heat produced.
Time (\(t\)) — longer time → greater heat produced.

notes.heading: 11.7.1 Practical Applications of Heating Effect of Electric Current

blocks.text: The heating effect of electric current is used in many electrical appliances.
Appliances such as electric heaters, electric irons and toasters use heating elements made of materials having high resistance. Nichrome is commonly used for heating elements because:

items: It has high resistivity.
It has a high melting point.
It does not oxidise easily at high temperature.
An electric fuse is a safety device used to protect electrical circuits from excessive current.
It contains a wire made of a material having high resistance and low melting point.
When excessive current flows, the fuse wire becomes very hot and melts, breaking the circuit.
This prevents damage to electrical appliances and wiring.
Heater/iron/toaster → Heating effect
Nichrome → Heating element
Fuse → Safety device
Excess current → Fuse melts → Circuit breaks

summary: Electric current (I = Q/t, in amperes) is the rate of flow of electric charge in a closed circuit, driven by potential difference (V = W/Q, in volts). An ammeter is connected in series to measure current, while a voltmeter is connected in parallel to measure potential difference. By Ohm's law, V = IR at constant temperature, where resistance R (in ohms, Ω) depends on conductor length, cross-sectional area, material and temperature according to R = ρl/A (with resistivity ρ in Ω m). Resistors in series carry the same current and have equivalent resistance R_s = R_1 + R_2 + R_3, while resistors in parallel share the same voltage and obey 1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3. By Joule's law of heating, heat produced in a resistor is H = I²Rt = VIt = V²t/R, which is applied in nichrome heating elements (electric heaters, irons, toasters) and safety fuses. Electric power is P = W/t = VI = I²R = V²/R (in watts, W), and electrical energy E = Pt is measured commercially in kilowatt-hours (1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 × 10⁶ J).

qa.q: Define electric current and 1 ampere, and state the relationship between conventional current and electron flow.
qa.a: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charges through a conductor (I = Q/t). One ampere is constituted by the flow of 1 coulomb of charge per second (1 A = 1 C s⁻¹). Conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, opposite to the actual flow of electrons.

qa.q: Define potential difference between two points and 1 volt. How is a voltmeter connected in a circuit?
qa.a: Potential difference (V = W/Q) is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to another. It is 1 volt when 1 joule of work is done to move 1 coulomb of charge (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹). A voltmeter is always connected in parallel across the component.

qa.q: How are an ammeter and a voltmeter connected in an electric circuit, and what does each measure?
qa.a: An ammeter measures electric current and is connected in series in the circuit. A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel across the two points.

qa.q: State Ohm's law, define 1 ohm, and describe the nature of the V–I graph for an ohmic conductor.
qa.a: Ohm's law states that at constant temperature, the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends (V = IR). One ohm (1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹) is the resistance of a conductor when 1 V potential difference produces 1 A current. Its V–I graph is a straight line passing through the origin.

qa.q: List the four factors on which the resistance of a conductor depends and write the formula relating resistance to resistivity.
qa.a: Resistance depends on (1) length of the conductor (R ∝ l), (2) area of cross-section (R ∝ 1/A), (3) nature of the material (resistivity ρ), and (4) temperature. Combining these gives R = ρ(l/A), where resistivity ρ has SI unit ohm-metre (Ω m).
qa.section: 11.5 Factors on which the Resistance of the Conductor Depends

qa.q: What is meant by the equivalent resistance of a system of resistors?
qa.a: Equivalent (or effective) resistance is the single resistance that can replace a series or parallel combination of resistors without changing the total current and voltage relationship in the circuit.
qa.section: 11.6 Resistance of a System of Resistors

qa.q: Write the formula for the equivalent resistance of three resistors connected in series and state which physical quantity remains constant across them.
qa.a: In series, the same electric current flows through every resistor, the total voltage is V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃, and the equivalent resistance is R_s = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ (which is greater than any individual resistor).

qa.q: Write the formula for the equivalent resistance of three resistors connected in parallel and state which physical quantity remains the same across them.
qa.a: In parallel, the same potential difference acts across each resistor, the total current is I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃, and the reciprocal of equivalent resistance is 1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ (so R_p is smaller than the smallest individual resistor).

qa.q: State Joule's law of heating and write the expressions for heat produced in a resistor.
qa.a: According to Joule's law of heating, the heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the square of the current (I²), the resistance (R), and the time (t) for which current flows: H = I²Rt = VIt = V²t/R.

qa.q: Why is nichrome used for heating elements, and how does an electric fuse protect a circuit?
qa.a: Nichrome has high resistivity, a high melting point, and does not oxidise easily at high temperatures. An electric fuse has a wire of high resistance and low melting point; when excessive current flows, it melts and breaks the circuit to prevent damage.
qa.section: 11.7.1 Practical Applications of Heating Effect of Electric Current

qa.q: Define electric power and its SI unit, and convert 1 kilowatt-hour (1 unit) into joules.
qa.a: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed: P = W/t = VI = I²R = V²/R. Its SI unit is watt (1 W = 1 V × 1 A). The commercial unit of electrical energy is kilowatt-hour (kWh), where 1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
